svg.title: Wiegand versus OSDP v2.2 reader-to-panel wiring
svg.desc: Side-by-side comparison of the two reader-to-panel protocols. Left, legacy Wiegand from 1974: one-way reader-to-panel signalling, no encryption on the wire, 26 and 37-bit formats with a 64-bit practical cap, exposed to ESPKey-class wire-tap devices, no tamper events or firmware path, 18 AWG six-conductor runs to about 500 feet. Right, OSDP v2.2: bidirectional RS-485 multi-drop, AES-128 Secure Channel, card formats up to 2048 bits, tamper monitoring and firmware updates over the wire, up to 32 readers per home-run, 22 AWG twisted pair to about 4000 feet. A banner underneath advises migrating at panel refresh with dual-output readers bridging the transition.
svg.text: READER-TO-PANEL PROTOCOL
Wiegand vs OSDP v2.2
The cheapest attack on a modern PACS is a fifty-year-old wire protocol.
Legacy Wiegand — 1974
One-way signalling: reader to panel only
No encryption anywhere on the wire
26 / 37-bit formats · 64-bit practical cap
ESPKey wire-tap captures every read
No tamper events, no firmware path
18 AWG 6-conductor · runs to ~500 ft
Still guarding a large share of installed doors —
which is exactly why attackers keep tooling for it.
OSDP v2.2 — SIA · IEC 60839-11-5
Bidirectional over RS-485 multi-drop
AES-128 Secure Channel on the wire
Card formats up to 2048 bits
Tamper monitoring + firmware update OTA
Up to 32 readers per home-run
22 AWG twisted pair · runs to ~4000 ft
Procure from the SIA OSDP Verified list —
and rotate the install-key off the factory default.
Migrate at panel refresh — dual-output readers bridge the transition
